proposal: The Mandate recommends that Congress cap the indirect (overhead) cost rate the federal government pays universities for research so that it does not exceed the lowest rate a university accepts from a private organization funding research. status_summary: No statute capping university indirect cost rates at a private-funder benchmark has been enacted; instead the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75, signed 2026-02-03) carries a bar on HHS developing or implementing a modified approach to indirect cost rates (Div. B sec. 224, per CRS), a grants consultancy summary reports that it also requires DoD to keep its existing rate framework (Div. A sec. 8146), and Public Law 119-103 (approved 2026-09-02) continues the fiscal year 2026 Acts' authority and conditions to 2026-12-11 at the latest, so the bars are inferred to remain in force under the continuing appropriations (an inference from section 101, which does not mention indirect costs). The executive branch pursued a different design, flat 15 percent caps: NIH issued NOT-OD-25-068 on 2025-02-07, DOE, NSF and DoD issued similar caps in April to June 2025, and courts blocked all four (NIH permanent injunction 2025-04-04, affirmed by the First Circuit on 2026-01-05; DOE preliminary injunction 2025-05-15; NSF policy vacated 2025-06-20; DoD preliminary injunction 2025-07-18), with ACE reporting on 2026-04-13 that the Justice Department did not seek Supreme Court review of the NIH ruling. The FY2027 budget again proposes a 15 percent NIH cap and removal of the bar. Because Congress, the actor the text names, enacted provisions that keep negotiated rates in place rather than a cap, the record is judged diverged.

timeline.event: NIH issued supplemental guidance NOT-OD-25-068 setting a 15 percent indirect cost rate for new and existing grants to institutions of higher education, for costs from 2025-02-10.
The D. Mass. court converted its preliminary relief into a permanent nationwide injunction against the NIH policy.
A federal judge in Massachusetts issued a nationwide preliminary injunction against the DOE 15 percent cap, replacing a temporary restraining order of 2025-04-16.
A D. Mass. judge granted summary judgment vacating the NSF 15 percent rate policy as arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law.
A D. Mass. judge issued a preliminary injunction against the DoD 15 percent cap, limited to the named universities and members of ACE, AAU and APLU.

The First Circuit affirmed the NIH ruling (Massachusetts v. NIH, No. 25-1343, with two related appeals), relying on recurring HHS appropriations language and on the Uniform Guidance as adopted at 45 CFR Part 75.
The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 became Public Law 119-75; per CRS, Division B section 224 carries the bar on HHS developing or implementing a modified approach to indirect cost rates.

A grants consultancy summary reported that P.L. 119-75 also requires DoD to keep applying its existing indirect cost rate framework and bars use of funds to change those rates (Div. A sec. 8146), alongside the HHS bar in Div. B sec. 224.
ACE reported that the Justice Department did not file a Supreme Court petition by its April 2026 deadline, leaving the First Circuit decision in place.
CRS reported that P.L. 119-75 continues the HHS indirect cost bar and that the FY2027 budget again proposes a 15 percent NIH cap and removal of the bar.

Public Law 119-103 (Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027) is approved. Division A section 101 continues funding at the fiscal year 2026 rate under the authority and conditions of twelve listed fiscal year 2026 Acts, including Public Laws 119-74 and 119-75, and section 106 ends that availability no later than 2026-12-11; Division A makes no reference to indirect cost rates.

title: Cap federal indirect cost rates for university research at the lowest private-funder rate
uncertainties: The Mandate asks Congress for a cap tied to the lowest rate a university accepts from a private funder; the 15 percent caps are a flat executive cap and are tracked as a parallel design. The section 224 citation rests on CRS and the section 8146 DoD provision on a consultancy summary. The govinfo.gov HTML and PDF of P.L. 119-75 were opened again on 2026-10-22 and still end within Division A (sections 8044 and 8072), so neither provision was read in statutory text; the provisions are uncodified, so no Code page applies. An external retrieval of the official enrolled text, not confirmed by an opened copy, reports the same section numbers and describes Division B section 224 as keeping the 45 CFR part 75 indirect cost provisions in force for NIH as applied in the third quarter of fiscal year 2017 and barring funds from being used to develop or implement a modified approach, in words that may reach funds of HHS or of any department or agency, and Division A section 8146 as requiring DoD to keep applying negotiated rates under 2 CFR 200.414 as applied in fiscal year 2024; the record keeps the HHS wording because section 224 was not opened. The same reading finds no percentage cap and no calendar end date in either section; both sit in the fiscal year 2026 act. Public Law 119-103 (approved 2026-09-02, opened on govinfo.gov) continues funding at fiscal year 2026 rates under the authority and conditions of the listed fiscal year 2026 Acts, which include Public Laws 119-74 and 119-75, until 2026-12-11 at the latest (section 106); that the two bars continue under it is an inference, since Division A mentions no indirect cost rates, and its section 157, which refers to a rule revising the Uniform Guidance, was not examined for any bearing on indirect costs. A fiscal year 2027 appropriations act would decide whether the bars continue beyond that date. The ACE page is an advocacy-group tracker and is the only source for the NSF and DoD dates and for the absence of a Supreme Court petition. The stage is a judgment call: blocked 10 is the alternative if the court-halted parallel executive caps are treated as the deciding action, while diverged follows if Congress's re-enacted bar is treated as the deciding action for a congressional ask.
